CAPSTONE PROJECT - SOCIAL MEDIA TOURISM¶

Problem Statement¶

An aviation company that provides domestic as well as international trips to the customers now wants to apply a targeted approach instead of reaching out to each of the customers. This time they want to do it digitally instead of tele-calling. Hence they have collaborated with a social networking platform, so they can learn the digital and social behavior of the customers and provide the digital advertisement on the user page of the targeted customers who have a high propensity to take up the product. Propensity of buying tickets is different for different login devices. Hence, you have to create 2 models separately for Laptop and Mobile.

NOTE: Anything which is not a laptop can be considered as mobile phone usage.

NOTE: The advertisements on the digital platform are bit expensive, hence you need to be very accurate while creating the models.

Renaming few of the columns for better readability and understanding:-¶

Replacing few long words in short abbreviations, like:

  • Travel_page and Company_page are same, so replacing it with: CP
  • Outstation or out of station are same, so replacing it with: OS
  • Yearly_avg as: YA
  • Daily_avg as: DA
  • Preffered as: Pref
  • Total_likes as: TL
  • Monthly_avg as: MA

We can see that there are various preferred location type available in the data. let us assign few of them into one category and organize these.

  1. We will take Beach, Historical site, Trekking, Tour Travel, Tour and Travel and Hill Stations in one category and will name it 'Adventure and Tourism'.

  2. We will be replacing Game, OTT, Movie and Social Media with one already available category 'Entertainment'.

Identifying Outliers with Interquartile Range :-¶

The interquartile range (IQR) is a measure of statistical dispersion and is calculated as the difference between the 75th and 25th percentiles. It is represented by the formula IQR = Q3 − Q1.

In [55]:
#Calculating Q1, Q3 and IQR values and assigning the upper limit (UL) and lower limit (LL)

Q1 = data[num_columns].quantile(0.25)
Q3 = data[num_columns].quantile(0.75)
IQR = Q3 - Q1
UL = Q3 + 1.5*IQR
LL = Q1 - 1.5*IQR
In [56]:
print('IQR values (Q3-Q1):\n\n',IQR)
print('\n_______________________\n')
print('Upper Limit (Q3 + 1.5*IQR):\n\n',UL)
print('_______________________')
print('Lower Limit (Q1 - 1.5*IQR):\n\n',LL)

Identifying Outliers with Skewness and Distribution Plot :-¶

Several machine learning algorithms make the assumption that the data follow a normal (or Gaussian) distribution. This is easy to check with the skewness value, which explains the extent to which the data is normally distributed. Ideally, the skewness value should be between -1 and +1, and any major deviation from this range indicates the presence of extreme values.

The rule of thumb seems to be: If the skewness is between -0.5 and 0.5, the data are fairly symmetrical. If the skewness is between -1 and – 0.5 or between 0.5 and 1, the data are moderately skewed. If the skewness is less than -1 or greater than 1, the data are highly skewed.

Outliers Treatment :- Using Quantile-based Capping and Flooring¶

In this technique, we will do the flooring (10th percentile) for the lower values and capping (90th percentile) for the higher values. These values will be used for quantile-based flooring and capping.

print('Flooring Values:\n\n',data[num_columns].quantile(0.10))

How many Laptop users have taken the product ??¶

In [92]:
data_laptop['Taken_product_Yes'].value_counts()
Out[92]:
0    832
1    276
Name: Taken_product_Yes, dtype: int64
In [93]:
data_laptop['Taken_product_Yes'].value_counts(normalize = True)
Out[93]:
0   0.75
1   0.25
Name: Taken_product_Yes, dtype: float64

832 laptop users (75%) has not taken the product and only 276 users (25%) has taken the product. This means that there is class imbalance in the dataset, where 1 is minority class and 0 is in majority class.

Need of applying SMOTE :-¶

As per our analysis, we got to know that the data is more towards the negative side, like majority of the users have not taken our product.This clearly means that data is in imbalance state.

Standard ML techniques such as Decision Tree and Logistic Regression have a bias towards the majority class, and they tend to ignore the minority class. They tend only to predict the majority class, hence, having major misclassification of the minority class in comparison with the majority class. In more technical words, if we have imbalanced data distribution in our dataset then our model becomes more prone to the case when minority class has negligible or very lesser recall.

So we will be using a over sampling technique called SMOTE to handle imbalanced data.

Logistic Regression Model (with default parameters) : On imbalance data¶

Before applying SMOTE on the data, we will first build the Logistic Regression Model on imbalanced data and will compare the performance of the the model with the other models on Balanced Data.

We can clearly see that the accuracy comes out to be 79% in test data and 85% in train data, but, the recall of the minority class in very less(38%). It means that the model is more biased towards majority class. So, it proves that this is not the best model, and it might be because of class imbalance. Now we will apply SMOTE - for Oversampling the minority class.¶

Now, Applying SMOTE :-¶

Now, we will apply the imbalanced data handling technique, called SMOTE and see their accuracy and recall results.

X_train, Y_train = SM.fit_sample(X_train, Y_train)

let us look at the Confusion Matrix, AUC- ROC Curve :-¶

AUC - ROC curve is a performance measurement for the classification problems at various threshold settings. ROC is a probability curve and AUC represents the degree or measure of separability. It tells how much the model is capable of distinguishing between classes. Higher the AUC, the better the model is at predicting 0 classes as 0 and 1 classes as 1. By analogy, the Higher the AUC, the better the model is at distinguishing between patients with the disease and no disease. The ROC curve is plotted with TPR against the FPR where TPR is on the y-axis and FPR is on the x-axis.

  • TPR (True Positive Rate) / Recall /Sensitivity = TP/(TP+TN)
  • Specificity = TN/(TN+FP)
  • FPR = 1-Specificity

Random Forest Classifier -¶

In [160]:
# Calling the Random Forest Classifier with hyper-parameters

rfcl = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=301,
                              oob_score = True,
                              max_depth = 10,
                              max_features = 5,
                              min_samples_leaf = 50,
                              min_samples_split=110)

rfcl = rfcl.fit(X_train, Y_train)

Hyper-parameters for the classifier :¶

  • n_estimators = number of trees, that we want to build within the RandomForestClassifier.

  • Out of bag (OOB) score is a way of validating the Random forest model. It is computed as the number of correctly predicted rows from the out of bag sample.

  • max_features will be used to select randomly features from the available number of features.

In [161]:
rfcl
Out[161]:
RandomForestClassifier(max_depth=10, max_features=5, min_samples_leaf=50,
                       min_samples_split=110, n_estimators=301, oob_score=True)

OOB Score (Out of Bag) and Error Rate for Random Forest Classifier -¶

The OOB score is computed as the number of correctly predicted rows from the out of bag sample.

In [162]:
rfcl.oob_score_

0.8163265306122449

For the above specified grid parameters, we got the Random Forest Model with OOB score around 81% and error rate around 19%, which shows the model is good to go for further evaluation.

Getting the Feature Importances :-¶

Feature Importance refers to techniques that calculate a score for all the input features for a given model — the scores simply represent the “importance” of each feature. A higher score means that the specific feature will have a larger effect on the model that is being used to predict a certain variable.

In [164]:

  • If we closely look at the Random Forest Model performance on test data, we get to find out that the recall value of minority class (1) is 76% while the accuracy is 80%, which is considerably a good result in comparison with the other previous models except the KNN model.

  • True Positive value here is 68 that means the model is able to predict 1 as 1 for 68 times out of 89, while False Negative value is 21 which means the model is predicting incorrectly 1 as 0 for only 21 times out of 89, which is good indicator but yet not the best.

  • If we look at the True Negative value where the actual is 0 and the predicted is also 0, it is 199, that means out of 244 zeros, 199 of the times the model is able to predict correctly and only 45 times the prediction is incorrect.

  • The model is good but not yet best. Now we will use some ensemble techniques like Bagging and Boosting to improve the performance of our model.

Gradient Boost -¶

  • Gradient boosting algorithm is one of the most powerful algorithms in the field of machine learning. As we know that the errors in machine learning algorithms are broadly classified into two categories i.e. Bias Error and Variance Error. As gradient boosting is one of the boosting algorithms it is used to minimize bias error of the model.

  • Unlike, Ada-boosting algorithm, the base estimator in the gradient boosting algorithm cannot be mentioned by us. The base estimator for the Gradient Boost algorithm is fixed and i.e. Decision Stump. Like, Ada-Boost, we can tune the n_estimator of the gradient boosting algorithm. However, if we do not mention the value of n_estimator, the default value of n_estimator for this algorithm is 100.

In [180]:
# Calling the Gradient Boost Classifier with it's own default base estimator and n_estimators =100 : 

gbcl = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators = 251, random_state=11)

# Fit the model on train data
gbcl = gbcl.fit(X_train, Y_train)

We can see that, out of 8499 mobile users, only 1278 (around 15%) has taken the product and 7221 (around 85%) has not taken the product.

Need of applying SMOTE :-¶

As per our analysis, we got to know that the data is more towards the negative side, like majority of the users have not taken our product.This clearly means that data is in imbalance state.

Standard ML techniques such as Decision Tree and Logistic Regression have a bias towards the majority class, and they tend to ignore the minority class. They tend only to predict the majority class, hence, having major misclassification of the minority class in comparison with the majority class. In more technical words, if we have imbalanced data distribution in our dataset then our model becomes more prone to the case when minority class has negligible or very lesser recall.

So we will be using a over sampling technique called SMOTE to handle imbalanced data.

Logistic Regression Model (with default values) : On imbalance data¶

We can see that model performs very bad on imbalanced data. The recall value for the minority class (1) is only 27% on test data. Hence now we will apply SMOTE (Oversampling) technique on imbalance data and make it balanced for better performance.

Applying SMOTE -¶

Now, we will apply the imbalanced data handling technique, called SMOTE and test it's accuracy and recall results.

In [204]:
SM = SMOTE(random_state = 2)

x_train, y_train = SM.fit_sample(x_train, y_train)

After OverSampling, the shape of y_train: (10084, 1)

Now the difference is clear, that after over-sampling, the accuracy has been reduced, but recall value is now much better than the model for imbalance data.

The accuracy of 73% is acceptable with good recall value for minority class, rather than the high accuracy with bad recall value. But now the precision value for minority class has reduced too much.

So here we will focus more on improving our recall and precision. Now, the recall for the minority class has been increased a lot, and it is very good. But the recall for the majority class has been decreased, this is due the fact that now that there is a balance in both the classes.

Logistic Regression Model (Customized Values) : On balanced data - After applying SMOTE - Oversampling¶

As we have build the previous model with it's default values. There might be chances of more better model than this, with some customized parameters for the logistic regression model.

We can improve the model by tuning the hyper-parameters of the model. So here we will use 'GridSearchCV' method to get the best parameters and then we would want to test out in the model again.

Random Forest Classifier -¶

In [242]:
# Calling the Random Forest Classifier with hyper-parameters

rfcl_mob = RandomForestClassifier(n_estimators=301,
                                  oob_score = True,
                                  max_depth = 10,
                                  max_features = 5,
                                  min_samples_leaf = 50,
                                  min_samples_split=110)

rfcl_mob = rfcl_mob.fit(x_train, y_train)

Hyper-parameters for the classifier :¶

  • n_estimators = number of trees, that we want to build within the RandomForestClassifier.

  • Out of bag (OOB) score is a way of validating the Random forest model. It is computed as the number of correctly predicted rows from the out of bag sample.

  • max_features will be used to select randomly features from the available number of features.

In [243]:
rfcl_mob
Out[243]:
RandomForestClassifier(max_depth=10, max_features=5, min_samples_leaf=50,
                       min_samples_split=110, n_estimators=301, oob_score=True)

OOB Score (Out of Bag) and Error Rate for Random Forest Classifier -¶

The OOB score is computed as the number of correctly predicted rows from the out of bag sample.

For the above specified grid parameters, we got the rfcl_mob model with oob score around 87% and error rate 13%, which shows the model is good to go for further evaluation.

Getting the Feature Importances :-¶

Feature Importance refers to techniques that calculate a score for all the input features for a given model — the scores simply represent the “importance” of each feature. A higher score means that the specific feature will have a larger effect on the model that is being used to predict a certain variable.

plt.xlabel("Random Forest Feature Importance")

  • If we closely look at the Random Forest Model performance on test data, we get to find out that the recall value of minority class (1) is 77% while the accuracy is 86%, which is a good result in comparison with the other previous models except the KNN model.

  • True Positive value here is 285 that means the model is able to predict 1 as 1 for 285 times out of 371, while False Negative value is 86 which means the model is predicting incorrectly 1 as 0 for 86 times out of 371, which is good indicator but yet not the best.

  • If we look at the True Negative value where the actual is 0 and the correct prediction has done, it is 1902, that means out of 2179 zeros, 1902 of the times the model is able to predict correctly and only 277 times the prediction is incorrect.

  • The model is good but not yet best. Now we will use some ensemble techniques like Bagging and Boosting to improve the performance of our model.

let us Now use Ensemble techniques : Bagging, Ada Boosting, GradientBoost :-¶

Gradient Boost¶

  • Gradient boosting algorithm is one of the most powerful algorithms in the field of machine learning. As we know that the errors in machine learning algorithms are broadly classified into two categories i.e. Bias Error and Variance Error. As gradient boosting is one of the boosting algorithms it is used to minimize bias error of the model.

  • Unlike, Ada-boosting algorithm, the base estimator in the gradient boosting algorithm cannot be mentioned by us. The base estimator for the Gradient Boost algorithm is fixed and i.e. Decision Stump. Like, Ada-Boost, we can tune the n_estimator of the gradient boosting algorithm. However, if we do not mention the value of n_estimator, the default value of n_estimator for this algorithm is 100.

In [266]:
gbcl_mob = GradientBoostingClassifier(n_estimators = 150,random_state=1)

# Fit the model on Train data

gbcl_mob = gbcl_mob.fit(x_train, y_train)
